newsitem.title: NORWAY: NATO ministers meet on Bosnia, reform.
newsitem.headline: NATO ministers meet on Bosnia, reform.

text.p: NATO defence ministers began talks on Wednesday on ways of extending peacekeeping in Bosnia into next year but the Americans, who would play a key role in any such force, have thrown in a word of caution.

The talks will offer the 16 ministers their first chance after the Bosnian elections on September 14 to discuss a follow-on force to stop the country sliding into war after the current mission's mandate ends in December.

The meeting will also discuss attempts to reform the alliance to enable it to carry it out more Bosnia-style tasks, take in new members from former communist Europe, and build a new relationship with Russia.
NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana said in an opening statement the meeting, which will take no final decisions, would be an opportunity "for us to clarify our thinking on issues facing us".

The allies agree some force has to remain in Bosnia in 1997 when the mandate for the current force, now numbering some 52,000, runs out in December, but the issue is highly sensitive in the U.S. ahead of November's presidential elections.

Norwegian Defence Minister Joergen Kosmo, who hosts the meeting, said in an opening statement: "I hope that through these political discussions we can make a consensus in such a way that our planners... can start real planning so we can show not only to ourselves but also to Europe and the world that NATO is ready to take action whenever needed."

But U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry, arriving on Tuesday for the meeting, voiced American caution over predictions by German Defence Minister Volker Ruehe and others that the NATO-led peace implementation force would indeed be replaced.
"I think all such judgments are premature. I really do," Perry said. "In the last analysis, they (other countries) will reserve their final judgment until they see what the requests are.
"I don't think we (the United States) can have a position until we see what the request is, what the mission is, what the force structure requested is."

The United States currently has 15,000 troops in Bosnia and President Bill Clinton and other administration officials have refused to predict any new mission next year ahead of a November presidential vote in the United States.)

Perry stressed to reporters travelling with him from Copenhagen on the last leg of a trip to four Nordic countries that no Bosnia decision would be made at the informal two-day NATO meeting in the old Hanseatic town of Bergen.

The defence chiefs, he said, would begin laying military plans and consider alternative strategies to prevent war from breaking out again in Bosnia. The proposals would be presented to the North Atlantic Council, the political arm of NATO, for a decision in December.
Ruehe said this week that he expected a new Bosnia mission to include 20,000 to 25,000 troops and that Germany was prepared to provide 2,000 to 3,000 of its own troops in such a force.
Norway, which has 1,000 troops in Bosnia, also said it wanted to contribute to an extended peacekeeping mandate.
But European allies have made clear they will not stay without a U.S. troop commitment.
Solana, and several European allies, have said openly the alliance will have to remain engaged beyond the end of the year, probably with a smaller force including U.S. troops.
Britain and France are adamant they will not remain if U.S. troops are not also present on the ground out of fear.

The ministers will also be able to meet new Russian Defence Minister Igor Rodionov, who on Thursday will sign an agreement with Perry and Norwegian Defence Minister Joergen Kosmo on tackling Russian military pollution in the Arctic.)
NATO's eastward expansion, a sensitive issue for the Russians, will be discussed on Thursday morning before the ministers go into a so-called 16+1 meeting with Rodionov, officials said.
